projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Michael K. Vitantonio was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Michael K. Vitantonio. Mr. Vitantonio served with the U.S. Marine Corps Third Marine Raider Battalion. He served in the Pacific theater, and his highest rank was staff sergeant.

I am Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Bob Miller's home in Willoughby, Ohio on May 21, 2001. Mr. Miller's World War II oral history was submitted on an earlier tape. And we recorded this during a rainstorm, and that is the white noise that you hear in the background of this tape. Michael Vitantonio's age at the time of this recording was seventy-eight.

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Getting back to the Marine Corps, name is Vitantonio, Michael K., USMC, 362429. And I remember when the war started, Japs attacked Pearl Harbor, which I don't think any of us knew where it was when it happened. I remember the seriousness of it, as it sank in on this Sunday.
I remember Monday morning, Congress met, Roosevelt got up there and told them, "I ask Congress to declare war". He said it would be a day that lived in infamy, and I remember all that.
And Tuesday morning, bright and early, I was down on west Third at the Engineers building, think it was the Engineers building, and I signed up in the Marine Corps then.

So, I was real proud of that, except that they were so crowded that they couldn't accept any of us to put us through the physicals and everything. And they had us all sign post cards, and they claim that when -- they would mail them to us when they were ready.

And so, a good buddy of mine that I grew up, Paul Blaise, he was called in January 4. I was called up February 4. And I signed up, if you notice, I emphasize USMC. There is no R after that. They asked us if we wanted to be a reserve or regular, and I asked what the difference was.
They said, well, a regular would be in for four years. A reserve would be in for the duration of the war, plus six months.
So, I, in my quick thinking, decided the war is going to last four years anyhow. So, I says I wanted to be a regular. And I am proud of it. I am glad I did.

And anyhow, I was sent to Parris Island, South Carolina, went through the boot training. It was accelerated in those days. We didn't have twelve, thirteen weeks. We had nine weeks. And then they took us, sent us up to Camp Lejeune, which wasn't really Camp Lejeune at that time. It was just barren fields. That's North Carolina. And they were building Cherry Point, Camp Lejeune. And they had buildings that were like pre-fabs, that you could punch your hand through. That's how thin it was. But it was better than tents.

And I remember qualifying in boot camp as a marksman, both rifle and pistol, which one thing they emphasize in the Marine Corps is everybody is a rifleman. And this is from the Commandant on down. Everybody has to go through the same boot training, you know. And you are a rifleman first. And then, from there on, any other thing you can do, typing or baking or auto mechanic, you know -- this is what I went into, as a secondary job like.

But anyhow, I finished up boot training, went up to Camp Lejeune. And the First Division was shipping out already. And they were going into Guadalcanal, which we didn't know at that time, but they were shipping out. And there were nine of us people that were -- like my last initial, or last name is Vitantonio, V. So, we were -- nine of us was supernumerary, they called us. They didn't need us in the books. So, they just took the division and they got them on board trains, and they went on to San Diego and overseas.
And there is nine of us, with nobody in charge, really. None of us were -- we all were PFC's then, I think. But there was no sergeant or anything in charge. And so, we just killed time.

We had nine vehicles to drive. One was a motorcycle. One was a half ton pickup. And we went to the regular mess hall to eat and everything. But like I say, we just drifted for a few days, quite a few days, until they start forming the next group. And that was the group we were put in.

And they shipped us out in early August, maybe even late July, but they put us on board a train that took five days to go across country. And in San Diego, we got off the train, right at the point where the ships were docked. And we went from the train across a bunch of railroad tracks, and on board ship.

It happened to be the USS Lureline. I called it USS, but it was Lureline. And it was a W.R. Grace line that had -- and it was -- at that time, it was the biggest cruise ship for the Pacific. And I guess it held two thousand people. Held fifteen thousand troops. And what they had done, they boarded up all the outer decks, you know, and everything, and stuck bunks in there, four feet -- four high. And I remember going in a convoy.

We took off, and we went to Pango Pango, Samoa, American Samoa. And that was my first stop overseas. We were there for approximately maybe five months, and we were trained -- I joined the Raider Battalion, Marine Raiders. There were four of our battalions formed, and we were trained to land from submarines in rubber boats. We would use an Evinrude four cylinder motor to get out to the submarine. And then, we would get on board the deck and then pull the boat up and then throw it back in, load back up, and then we'd paddle in. That was what we were trained to do, paddle silently, you know.

And actually, we never landed in -- they didn't use us as such. Only one battalion, the Second, went in the Macon Island that way. And they went ashore in two subs. Can't remember, one was a Nautilus. Oh, and the other I think was the Argonaut. And these were World War I submarines, so the poor guys must have had it rough going in, you know. And that was really the only time they used us to land from rubber boats. The rest of us went in on regular, what they call APAs. And we landed in LSTs and small Higgins boats.

So, anyhow, from American Samoa, we went to Guadalcanal. And we were in the last two weeks of Guadalcanal before they declared it secure. So, I got to see Henderson Field, and never got to fire at anybody. We didn't see any enemy. Although we had to be ready because when they call it secure, they are not really secure. I mean there is still remnants, you know. And we had to be prepared for that.

Anyhow, we spent a few more weeks getting ready. And the next thing you know, we went up north to Russell Island, which is the further -- I mean the further north that we have ever been against the Japs, you know. Guadalcanal was first, Tulagi, and then the Russell Island was the next group north, which we took. And we were strafed by Japs there. They -- planes, they come by and they spotted a couple of our Higgins boats in the bay. And I don't -- I think they were surprised. They didn't know what was going on, but they -- we were in a coconut grove. That's where we set up our tents and everything. And they strafed us there. So, that was the first time we were under fire. I remember shooting back at them. I know I didn't hit anything. And I saved the shells, you know, the shell casings. I must have saved them for almost the whole time I was in the Pacific.

Then, from there, we come back to Guadalcanal. That was our staging area. That's where we got replacements of equipment, men that we lost, and we lost a lot. Not necessarily wounded, but -- and killed. We lost a lot to malaria, things like that. Dengue fever.
So then, from there, we sent up a group, which I was what we call post-troops. I stayed on Guadalcanal, but half of our outfit went up to New Georgia, which was the next island group up.

And then, when they come back, we regrouped again, new equipment and stuff. And then, we went up to Bougainville. We landed there November 1st of I think '43. And I remember -- oh, then we come back from there. We -- most of the time, we would only stay -- well, some places, we stayed ten days; but on Bougainville, I believe we stayed about a month, a month and a half. And then, the army always come in, and they were post-troops afterward. They took over and kept the place going.

And we come back from there. And a couple times we went down to -- from Guadalcanal, we went down to New Hebrides and New Caledonia. Again, they were used as staging areas, you know. And then, we went to an island called Arovo. It was a real gem. Every time I think of the movie South Pacific, I think of this island. It had to be about three miles by five miles, is all the biggest it was. But it was just beautiful, gorgeous. The water around it was, you know, the blue, the green, and all the different colors. And of course, no Japs were there, but we found their equipment. And I remember there was some shooting going on. And what it was is the destroyers were getting in as close as they could get, and they assumed the Japs were on the other side, and they start firing. And of course, it was our own ships firing at each other.

And the only casualty that I can remember, I wasn't there, so just as hearsay, but I remember that one of the demolition men took off his pack, and he dropped it, and it blew him and the pack up, because they carried the detonators in the packs, you know. But that's about the only thing there.

But all I can remember, the island was fabulous. And we found a lot of Jap equipment. It was a radio place for them. And what the government was doing at that time, we were trying to get landing fields all around New Ireland and Truk, all these different islands that had big concentrations of Japs. And basically, that's what they should have done most of the time, bomb the places instead of going in. We find out afterward a lot of these islands were taking terrible casualties, and no reason to be taking it all, you know. Peleliu was one of them that keeps coming up now that they shouldn't even have gone into it.

So, then again, we come back to Guadalcanal as a staging area. And then, the next operation was -- for me was Guam. And we took that. We landed on my birthday of '44. July 21 -- 20. The date line messes me up on that.

But I remember having a brand new wrist watch my folks sent me, and it had on it "waterproof". And as we went ashore, everybody fanned out from the Higgins boat, you know. They drop the front down, and we all fanned out so that they could bring -- we had 37 millimeter antitank guns. We had twelve of them and twelve Dodge pickups that towed them. And they were -- you know, we had one in every boat like.
And so, what happened there is they had us fan out. And then, wherever the guys would say well, it was okay to come, follow me like, they would do that.

Well, I took off one direction, I stepped in a shell hole under water, and I remember going down, of course, and the watch full of water. It didn't last long after that. I saved it, but it wasn't worth repairing, you know.

And Guam was where we -- our outfit lost two good buddies, guy named PFC -- huh. Oh, boy. I hate to say I am forgetting his name, but I did. Momentarily, anyhow. But anyhow, we lost a sergeant, too, Sergeant Graves. But this PFC from New Jersey, he was going by in front of a Jap cave. And the Japs inside the cave, you know, he was silouetted. It was easy to shoot at him. And they killed him. And when Sergeant Graves heard about it, he went up to get the body, and they killed him, too.
So, what we did then, we all pulled back, and we had demolition go in and blew up the front of the cave and left them there. Although pretty sure they had other ways out, you know.

But I remember basically Guam was mostly where we were under fire. The first night we were there, everybody dug foxholes like we are trained to do. And I thought I was going to weasel out and not dig one. I was going to sleep in the back of the shop truck. And we had acetylene and oxygen tanks sticking up. And I decided I was going to sleep in the back of the truck. And so, I made a couple of cushions like all in there, and made a little nest, you know. And I -- we had canvas over the whole back.

So, we all went in to bed for the night, and posted our guards and -- right on the sea shore. We were just off where the scrub grass was. And I remember, as we landed, I mean it was like a panorama, if you want to use that term. We could just see the first and second line of troops going in. And you could actually see the Japs and all throwing grenades, and our guys throwing grenades back, shooting at each other. It went up a hillside. And we landed south of Orote Peninsula. And the main body of our group, Third Division, they landed on the northern side where the capital, Agana, Guam was. But we landed on the southern part. And what we were supposed to do, and which we did, is as we landed, we were supposed to make a left turn and go out to Orote Peninsula and recapture the marine base there.

And that was a sort of a prideful thing that we wanted to do, and we did. But like I say, this was a beautiful view of what was going on, and it was just like in the movies. A lot of -- lot of shooting up going, and all that sort of stuff.

So, anyhow, that first night, we dug in for the night, and we could hear the Japs. I am almost sure they were getting drunk on sake, you know. And could hear them talking away. And I sort of, you know, had to be quiet. You never knew what was going on exactly, but you could hear them yakking away, yakking away.

And early in the morning, they would come down a draw. You could hear the swords and all kinds of noise. They sure weren't quiet. And they come down, and they attacked us. And of course, didn't know what was going on until the shooting started. And they claim that they drove our guys right down to the water before they were able to regroup and come back. And I never got a shot off. I kept poking out of the canvas, just to see what was what. And I never got a shot off, not one round.

And I woke up in the morning, everything was quiet. I start hearing talking, the guys. And I heard, sixteen dead Japs all around my truck. And I had bullet holes in the truck. It was lucky none of them hit the acetylene or oxygen because those are real projectiles. But I remember that happening. I was embarrassed, as I had slept in the truck then, you know. But we just tied ropes around their ankles and dragged them. And we had one of those DC 8's, I guess they call them, Caterpillar, come by, and he just dug a big ditch. We dragged the Japs over to it and buried them and went on about our jobs, you know.
But when that was over, we come back, and to Guam -- or rather Guadalcanal. And got ready for the next one, which I didn't know at the time, but it was Okinawa.

So, they come back. They asked us if anybody with twenty-four months or more wanted to come back home or stay. And if we would have stayed, we would go up another rank. I was a four striper, so I would have been a staff sergeant, five. But I decided I wanted to come home.

I hadn't been wounded, at all. I had a Dengue fever. I also had an arm swell up, and I had the doctor punch a hole in it to drain it. And that's the only scar I have. Well, it isn't the only. I have three. I have on my head, diving in the creek on Guadalcanal, it was too shallow. I hit bottom.

And then, I have a scar right here on my left hand. I had to train a guy to drive our trucks, you know. They were all stick shifts. And I was training a guy with one of the Dodge pickups. And he must have went one way or the other, and I reached over and grabbed the emergency. And we had map boards that were under the dash, pull out to use. And must have had metal clips on it, because when I pulled back on it, I scratched my hand there on the metal clip.
But that was all. I had the three scars, and that's it. So, I decided well, I am not going to wait for the fourth one. And I decided to come back home.

Going back to Guam again, when we left, every time we got ready to leave an island, we had to kind of -- the ships were loaded, and then we stayed in the harbor until we formed groups to get a convoy started. And they always had to leave the harbor at 6:00 all the time. That's the latest. And then, they put the torpedo nets back across the openings.

So, we left Guam to come back to Guadalcanal. And we were on some kind of a ship, a danish ice breaker, had a real curved prow, wide staircase. Nothing like on board our ships, you know, with the narrow gangways. And I remember we left the harbor, formed a convoy, and then away we went. And then, all of a sudden, our ship had a big flare up out of the smoke stack. And everybody was kind of frightened about -- what's that?

And they said well, it was soot in the -- in the funnel, you know. So, turned out that whoever the crew was -- which we had a mixture. We always had navy gun crews, but they were -- you know, this happened to be a danish ice breaker, and it was running by somebody, and some other group, maybe British. And then, we had, say, Filipinos or something for crew. It was all mixed up, motley group. And they didn't clean the funnels. They let them flare up like that, you know.

So, that -- we figured, boy, the Japs are going to see us, you know. So, anyhow, we took off. And we weren't too far out, time wise, but it was getting dark. And the funnels flared up again, you know. And what we had decided was, we are not going to sleep below deck. We are going to sleep above.
So, everybody was trying to ferret out a place to sleep. And this one guy, PFC Bankhead, he went up somewhere where the life boats were, and he found a spot, lay down on his life jacket.
In those days, we had the Kapok, and we also had the small waist -- dioxide tubes, you know, capsules.

So, anyhow, he had the kapok, and made a good pillow for him. And he decided to sack out up there. And he fell asleep. We all did, you know, wherever we were. And he says he remembers that this thing flared up. And of course, he was sound asleep. So, when he saw that, woke him up, he was really scared, you know. And I don't know what he did, moving wise, but anyhow, he fell overboard.

Now, this actually happened because I know the guy. I know him real well. Turns out he fell overboard. He had his jacket with him, his life jacket. And he says he was swimming and trying to yell, you know, but the ship just went right on by him, and nobody else knew he was over there. So, nobody looked for him.
So, we have roll call regularly on board ship. Anywhere we are, we have roll car regular. I would guess we -- three times a day. In the morning, sometime during the middle of the day, and at night.
So, as soon as morning came, they had roll call. No PFC Bankhead.
So, right away, they radioed Guam, says send out some planes to look for him. And they found him the next day at four o'clock in the afternoon.

He had presence of mind. He says the kapok lasted a couple hours, and then sank. But he had presence of mind, just lay on his back and float. And he was light skinned, so he was really suffering from the sun. But they found him. They picked him up, brought him back to Guam, and then he joined our outfit about three months later. It was really remarkable, you know.

So, anyhow, I'd say -- let's see. After Guam, that was it. I had, don't know, twenty-eight months, something like that by then, and got to come home, and I did. I come back to the States. Can't remember the name of the ship. Took two weeks. We landed in San Diego on Thanksgiving Day of 1944. And essentially, my war was over then, which was a great relief to me, although I didn't know it. We were all told you have six months maximum in the States, and then you are going back over again.

So, my orders were to report to Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. And while I was home on thirty day furlough, I got a telegram from the War Department saying that orders are modified. Report to Crane Naval Ammunition Depot in Indiana.
So, I didn't know where Crane was. And I went down to the train station and asked them to give me a ticket to there. And nobody knew where it was.

So, sometime during the time I was down there, some old timer come in. They used to come down and spend the day there, I guess, pass away time, retirees, you know. And finally, one of them thought -- one of the ticket guys thought to ask him, and he says "would you know where this is?" And he knew right away. It was called Burns City. And you know, I don't even know if it was on the map, but they changed it from Burns City to Crane, and that's why they got messed up.

So, anyhow, he says "give the fellow a ticket to Terre Haute", says "have him take a bus to Bloomington, Indiana", which is Bloomington University. And he says "the Marine bus will pick him up there". And that's exactly what happened. The Marine bus met me in Bloomington, took me to the base. And my last thirteen months in the service were spent there in Indiana, which I thought the world of. I thought it was a terrific state. People were great. It was beautiful in the spring and fall. And the duty was great. We had beautiful barracks, swimming pool, PX. We had the whole bit, you know. And this is just for us enlisted men.

So, I think -- I almost shipped over. I was, I'd say, within an eighth of an inch of signing up again because I loved the Marine Corps. And I think most of us did. And to this day, I still keep track and touch with the guys that I was with. There is only a few of us left, but I used to have like twenty-four to twenty-six names. I am down to about maybe -- maybe if I am lucky, maybe ten, twelve now. Most of the guys are gone. One of them, the closest one, is from Steubenville, real good buddy of mine, Miklas. And I see him roughly ever other year, something like that. I go down for the day. And I am godfather to one of his boys. He had a son that, an older boy, Ted, that joined the Marines after college. And he worked his way up to major, Major Miklas. Ted Miklas. And he got his twenty years in, and then he retired.
But all in all, I mean I don't regret it. In fact, I loved the idea of being in the Corps. If it weren't for boot camp, I'd do it again. Oh, man.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I hated boot camp, too.

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: That was tough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did any of your buddies sign up for the Okinawa tour?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Oh, most of them did. Because see, we went over right away, the first group. And most of the other guys came over later, they didn't have twenty-four months. Miklas was one of them that stayed over. Quite a few.

And one of them, Don May, he lives in Unadilla, New York state now. He stayed in for thirty years. And he -- he is from Akron. But he married a girl that he met, American girl, down in Bogota, Colombia. And he was on what they call legation duty. He is one of these guys, he would be a picture perfect marine, you know, for photos and things like that. He just looks like a marine. And he met his wife down there when he was legation duty, and they got married. And I don't know who -- whether she is from that area or what, but they happened to move to Unadilla, New York. And he is one of them that I can remember that stayed the whole time. And he was on recruiting duty for a while, too. Again, they pick these guys that look good, you know. And they should.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, you were stateside on VE Day and VJ Day?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: I was in the States, and I was walking guard duty both times. I can remember that. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular celebrations you remember?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Well, no. Because I was on base, you know. And if we were able to get into town or something, we probably would have enjoyed it, but I was just glad it was over. Both times, you know. And that not having to go back overseas was a real relief.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Don't think we got your specific unit, and the breakdown. The unit you were in?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Well, actually, I was in the Third Battalion of the Marine Raiders. And it lasted a year and a half. And they -- hire ups, you know, they thought that what we are doing here is we are forming a super marine group, and they didn't want that. So, there were enough opposition in probably the army and everybody else, too, plus in the Marine Corps, that they wanted to eliminate us, so they did.

But Colonel Jimmy Roosevelt, you know, his son, one of Roosevelt's sons, he was one of us. He ended up in charge of the Fourth Battalion. And it was great while it lasted. We got special -- we were first to have camoflauge green uniforms. They were issued to the four battalions first. And then, as they made more of them, then the whole Marine Corps got them. Because up until then, we had tan.

And we were issued special stilettos. I wished I'd have kept mine but, you know, they make you turn everything in after every operation, and you get all new equipment. Except your rifle. Your rifle is your life, and you kept that all -- all the time. I can't remember the number there. I just remember my serial number, but I used to know the bayonet number and the rifle number. They made you remember everything. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any souvenir gathering that you remember?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Souvenir what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: American reputation of gathering souvenirs in the battle field, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: No, I didn't save anything. Except, like I mentioned, those shell casings, you know, for a while. And then, after a while, we were shooting so much, you just didn't bother.

But I had a buddy of mine that was one of these that he was a souvenir hound from Boston, Massachusetts. And he was a comedian. He was really a riot. He could remember jokes. He'd keep -- we'd dig foxholes all around his foxhole in the center. And all the night long, when he could, you know, "Did you ever hear this one?" And then, he would start on. But he can go all night long. He just had one after the other. Gus Greeley. And he passed away a while back, but he was a souvenir hound from out of this world.

In fact, after the war, he opened up a -- not a curio shop, but a souvenir thing. And he had -- I saw this. His dad had the Allied Moving Van franchise in Boston, 32 George Street. I still remember it. And I visited him a few times, and he took me down there. And he had souvenirs from the Germans and the Japs. And I remember he had some parachutes. I don't know whose they were. But anyhow, he had them hanging from the top.

He had some small tank, actual metal, you know, real live tank. Whether it was ours or German, I don't know which. But he had that in his -- he had two or three of these big rooms, you know. But he had all kinds of stuff. I mean, he had Jap stuff, our stuff, and I suppose Australian. But he really went for the souvenirs.

Most of the time, he had his rifle on upside down on his shoulder, you know. We usually keep it right side up. He had his upside down. He had a screwdriver and a pair of pliers. He'd be looking for anything with Japanese writing on it. And he would be stripping it. Because in those days, they had steamrollers like, the Japs did, that would look like they were first ones designed and built, you know, 1900. But they got things done. You got to hand it to them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did he ship the stuff back?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Oh, he had boxes all made already before we landed. And then, he would carry some with him, and he would pay these coxswains, navy coxswains that handle the Higgins boats, and he would pay them.

What he would do, like he would make arrangements ahead of time. And when we would go ashore, he would get whatever he could, put it in a box, and then he'd hand it to them. And then, they would go back to the ship, and they would make sure it goes into the post office on board ship like.

And then, of course, it wasn't -- I don't think they even censored any of that stuff, you know, because they were handling wounded and all back, so they didn't bother with that. And he sent a lot of stuff home.
If it wasn't -- then we had another buddy from Brooklyn, too. And if it wasn't for these guys and this buddy from Steubenville, I think we'd have all gone berserk over there.

But these guys were just so funny, so witted, so natural, you know. And I think that's one of the reasons why I feel so close to the Marine Corps today. First off, we were trained to cover each other's back. And you all was buddied up with somebody, you know. And you trusted him, and he trusted you. If you were assigned to a foxhole and told to stay there, no matter what, well, you can be sure the next morning when you woke up, if you even got a wink of sleep, but you can be sure that he is going to be in the hole with you. He isn't going to bug out, you know. And he might be dead, but he is going to still be there.
And that was the nice feeling, you know, of protection and stuff. I loved the Corps.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank then?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Well, I made it up to this fifth stripe, which would have been a tech sergeant. And then, they took it back. And says "Okay, you can go home, you know".
So, I would say -- what happened, they stripped me back to my last organizational -- these were organizational warrant ones. They stripped me of my last permanent warrant, which was corporal.

So, when I come back from overseas, I was drawing fairly decent money there with combat pay, you know. And then, I come back, and they stripped me down to corporal. I made $66 a month. So, that was a tough blow. But I was like Fred. We never drank, never swore, never --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You swear now?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: I was going to say never chase women, ha ha ha.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Get any medals or anything?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: No. All they -- you know, the standard ribbons. I don't think I ever got any, you know. I mean, we would have known. In fact, not too long ago, my boy sent in a request for like a review of what we have, you know. It goes to St. Louis somewhere. And I signed the papers, and we sent it in. So, hopefully, they let me know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any trouble adapting to civilian life afterward?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: No, not a bit, huh-uh. I almost, like I mentioned, I almost went back in. I decided after I was back, maybe let's see, February, I would guess a month, I asked my dad if I could use the car. We only -- that was the only car we ever had, a '36 Ford we picked up in 1941 for $200, ha ha. And I told him I'd like to go back around the country and visit the different buddies of mine.
And then, I had a sister and brother-in-law living out in LA. So, mom and dad says "go ahead and take the car", you know. He is used to walking to work and taking a streetcar.

So, I end up -- ended up in March, March 15, I left. And I was going to take a buddy or two, but they all chickened out at the last minute. So, I ended up, I piled my clothes in the car, and I drove back to Indiana. I stayed on the base there for two weeks. I ate in the mess hall, wore Marine uniform and everything. And the officers spent a lot of time with me. In fact, I was invited over to each of their houses, you know, at different days. I think they wanted to really sign me up again. And I come real close.

But then, I took off from there, went to Route 66 in St. Louis, and I took that all the way to, the southern route, to LA. I visited different places there. Can't remember exactly what town. Tucumcari, Flagstaff, things like that. And I got to LA, visited with my sister and brother-in-law, stayed there a couple of weeks.

And then, from there, I come back to the northern route, and I visited Marine buddies all along the way, you know. And stayed two weeks in South Dakota, Beresford, South Dakota, helped build a dairy barn for one of the guys' father-in-law's. I got a picture of me on top of this roof. How I ever got there, I don't know. Today, I wouldn't even go up a step ladder even anymore. But here I was on top of the roof helping to shingle it.

And then, I come back, I think April, May. Oh, I was gone three months. March, April, May, June. So, I come back when this good buddy of ours, Manuel Martinez, he got married, and I came back the day before that. I didn't know he was getting married, but I was able to make the wedding.
So, then, it turned out I stayed in until the February 4, 1946, and that finished my four years. And I was discharged from Indiana.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Mail call, letter memories?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: I am glad you mentioned that because that was one thing. I still have almost all the letters that were -- that I sent. My folks saved everything. And I have most of my letters.
When I got out of school, I went to the CCCs, and it was stationed in Utah near Wendover, Utah. We were 86 miles from there. That was the nearest town.
And then, when I come back from there, then I started to work in the general repair garage downtown, and then the war started. And that's when I signed up.

So, anyhow, my folks gave me all my letters and stuff like that back. And I still have them up in the attic. I never sorted them out, but it is amazing that I still have them. I don't know if they will do anybody any good, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It would be fascinating.

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: CCC's?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was that?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Civilian Conservation Corps.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what I just wanted to make sure.

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Uh-huh, yeah. They asked me when I signed up, I -- I couldn't find a job right away when I got out of school, you know. I didn't think to apply like these guys all did. They went to Tapco and Warner and Swazey and all that. Bailey Meter, Reliance. But I mean I ended up -- was trying to find a place to start being a mechanic, you know.
So, anyhow, I couldn't find a job that quick, and I decided I'd join the CCC's. And they asked me "where do you want to go? Do you want to stay in Ohio or you want to travel?"
I says "I want to travel".

So, they sent me to Utah. And I got a kick out of that because when we were sent there, we went to Salt Lake City first and got off the train, and it was an army base, Fort Douglas. And these guys, you know, you could tell they resented you. And you wonder why don't they like us? I mean, we don't even know them. Turned out that the army was still getting $21 a month, and they were paying us guys thirty bucks a month. But we only got eight dollars out of it. Twenty-two had to come home to your family. That was more or less to keep us off street corners, I guess, you know.
But I like the CCC's, and it was a perfect beginning for the service, you know. They trained you in hygiene and how to make your beds and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So, your job was rifleman/mechanic?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In the military?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: What they did, they asked if anybody had any experience at something. Well, I really didn't have much as a mechanic, but I mean that's what my trend was. So, I wrote down, you know. Everybody is considered a rifleman. A cook is a rifleman. Because that's the training we go through. You are rifleman first, and then you do anything else as a sideline, you know.

And that was -- I think the Marine Corps has the right way to go. They can -- if something -- just say for example if you are working in the artillery end of it. If the enemy were to overrun your positions and all that, with your experience as rifleman, you know, you just automatically go back to that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything come to mind -- anything else come to mind as a distant memory of the experience?

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Of the service?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael K. Vitantonio
sp.p: Well, besides the guy falling overboard. I remember the first time we were under fire was at Russell Island with the Japs strafing us. And then, on Bougainville, the surf was so high going into the mainland of Bougainville, we had to land at an island offshore called Hurata. And I went up on an LST and, you know, those great big opening front and everything, and they drop us off there. And then, we had to stay on that island for a couple of nights until they were ready for us on the mainland. At night, the Japanese would send over what we call Washer Machine Charlie, and he comes over in this -- I think it was a sea plane of some type. But it was a real old noisy thing. And it would always wake you up if you were trying to sleep. And as soon as he'd come over, you could hear him coming and all. Then the search lights would be going up, and they'd pounce on him, you know, and he'd be gleaming up above you, going real slow. The whole idea was to keep you disturbed where nobody got any rest. And then, he would throw some bombs, drop some bombs now and then. And I can remember our antiaircraft shooting at him. And all this stuff coming down really wasn't from Jap bombs, which we thought it was, you know. You can hear them drop here and there. And I don't think I ever was as frightened as I was that night. I bit a hole in my blanket, and a piece of shrapnel landed on the sand bags about a foot from my head, you know. And I can remember, I dug that piece out and saved it, too, but I don't think it was from the Jap bomb. I believe what it was was our own antiaircraft shooting practically straight up, and then all the shrapnel coming down. But there was so many ways like, you know, I am sure we lost guys to accidents. I can remember sitting in a Jeep, and we had these armored -- they were Amp Tracks, we called them. And they had cleats for the traction, you know. And they were coming down the road. And the guy driving them can't see too well. They got their head popping out just halfway. And I can remember being in a Jeep, and it was parked somewhere on the road. And this thing come up. And we figured the guy driving, he could see. Well, he must not have seen it because he started to come up on to the Jeep. He got on to the bumper, you know, and everything, and the Jeep is going down, and I am sitting in the passenger side. And I figured for sure I was going to get run over, but two things. I up and took off. And then he stopped, also, then backed up, you know. But you know, if you had had a casualty there. So, I -- like Bob mentioned, we'd lose people to friendly fire, friendly everything.
